papers.title: Estimación del riesgo a la salud por exposición laboral a pesticidas utilizados en el control de vectores en México
papers.abstract: El uso de pesticidas en México se ha promovido ampliamente para el control y combate de vectores que transmiten enfermedades víricas como chikungunya, dengue, paludismo y zika, que actualmente constituyen un problema de salud pública en el país, siendo el sector laboral dedicado a la aplicación de estos productos la población más expuesta. En el presente estudio se estimó el riesgo para la salud por exposición ocupacional a los principales pesticidas utilizados para el control de vectores de enfermedades, recomendados por el Centro Nacional de Programas Preventivos y Control de Enfermedades (CENAPRECE) y potencialmente tóxicos para los seres humanos (bifentrina, pirimifos-metil y bendiocarb). Para ello, se identificaron sus posibles efectos sobre la salud considerando su potencial tóxico (pT) y neurotóxico (pNe), así como la dosis de exposición estimada (DEE) en el ámbito laboral, de acuerdo con los años de exposición. Se determinaron el riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI). Se encontró que el bendiocarb presentó los valores más altos de riesgo de efectos no cancerígenos sobre la salud (HQ > 1 = riesgo alto), con incrementos significativos de 1.35, 2.7 y 4.1 conforme aumentaron los años de exposición laboral (5, 10 y 15 años, respectivamente). Por su parte, la bifentrina y el pirimifos metil mostraron incrementos proporcionales al tiempo de exposición laboral, pero con valores de HQ < 1 (bajo riesgo). Por lo tanto, el bendiocarb es el pesticida que representa la mayor preocupación para la salud. Sin embargo, no se deben descartar los otros dos compuestos, ya que puede haber un riesgo acumulado. Esto se debe a que los tres pesticidas pueden afectar el mismo órgano o sistema de órganos.

analysis.research_question_and_background: El estudio aborda el problema de la exposición laboral a pesticidas utilizados en el control de vectores de enfermedades víricas, como el chikungunya, en México, donde estos agentes constituyen un desafío de salud pública. El objetivo es evaluar el riesgo sanitario asociado con el uso de estos pesticidas en el ámbito laboral.
analysis.study_design_and_population: El estudio se enfoca en la evaluación del riesgo de salud por exposición ocupacional a pesticidas utilizados para el control de vectores de enfermedades víricas en México. Se consideraron los principales pesticidas recomendados por el CENAPRECE, incluyendo bendiocarb, bifentrina y pirimifos-metil, que son potencialmente tóxicos para los seres humanos.
analysis.methods: Se identificaron los efectos sobre la salud de los pesticidas considerando su potencial tóxico (pT) y neurotóxico (pNe), así como la dosis de exposición estimada (DEE) en el ámbito laboral, de acuerdo con los años de exposición. Se calculó el riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI) para cada pesticida.
analysis.main_results: El bendiocarb mostró los valores más altos de riesgo de efectos no cancerígenos sobre la salud, con HQ > 1 (riesgo alto) y incrementos significativos de 1.35, 2.7 y 4.1 conforme aumentaron los años de exposición laboral (5, 10 y 15 años, respectivamente). La bifentrina y el pirimifos metil presentaron incrementos proporcionales al tiempo de exposición laboral, pero con valores de HQ < 1 (riesgo bajo).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Los resultados indican que el bendiocarb representa el mayor riesgo para la salud en comparación con los otros dos pesticidas, lo cual es una observación directa basada en los cálculos de riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Estos hallazgos pueden informar la necesidad de implementar medidas de protección más estrictas para los trabajadores expuestos al bendiocarb, así como guiar la selección de pesticidas en programas de control de vectores de enfermedades víricas en México.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: El estudio se basa en datos abstractos y no proporciona información detallada sobre la metodología o controles utilizados, lo que limita la confianza en los resultados. Sin embargo, los hallazgos son directos y se basan en cálculos de riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI), lo que justifica una evaluación de confianza moderada.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the health risk associated with occupational exposure to pesticides used for vector control in Mexico, focusing on those relevant to chikungunya virus transmission. The research identifies bendiocarb as the pesticide with the highest non-cancerous health risk, based on calculated hazard quotients (HQi) and risk indices (HI), which increase significantly with years of exposure. Bifenthrin and pirimiphos-methyl show proportional increases in risk but remain at lower levels. The findings highlight the need for stricter protective measures for workers exposed to bendiocarb and inform the selection of pesticides in vector control programs. However, the study is limited to abstract-level data, and the evidence is considered moderate in strength due to the lack of detailed methodology and controls.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 研究人员研究了墨西哥基孔肯雅热病害防治中使用 媒介 杀虫剂控制害虫的劳动问题,旨在解决公共健康问题。我们的目的是评估卫生协会在工作中使用杀虫剂的情况。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们致力于对墨西哥的 媒介 病毒防治职业病害防治状况进行评估。请考虑 CENAPRECE 推荐的主要杀虫剂,包括苯虫威、联苯三唑和吡咪磷,对人体具有潜在的毒性。
elements_zh.methods: 识别潜在毒性 (pT) 和神经毒性 (pNe) 的害虫防治效果,并根据暴露估计剂量 (DEE) 和劳动强度,快速应对暴露情况。可以计算出没有癌症基因的个体 (HQi) 和有杀虫剂的个体 (HI)。
elements_zh.main_results: 苯硫卡最重要的价值是无癌症的健康,与 HQ > 1 (riesgo alto) 和 1.35、2.7 和 4.1 的显着增量一致,符合劳动日的 años de exosición 劳动(分别为 5、10 和 15 年)。La bifentrina y el pirimifos metil Presentaron Incrementos Incrementos Al tiempo de exposición Laboral,pero con valores de HQ < 1 (riesgo bajo).
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 印度苯虫威的结果代表了市长对其他杀虫剂的健康比较,通过直接观察来计算没有癌症的个人 (HQi) 和国家 (HI)。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 我们将通知您对使用双效苯乙威的工人实施保护措施的必要性,并根据墨西哥 媒介 病毒控制计划选择杀虫剂。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 我们的研究涉及抽象数据,并且没有详细说明控制使用方法的比例信息,但限制了结果的机密性。禁运,我们的指导方针是对个人癌症基因计算 (HQi) 和癌症指数 (HI) 进行计算,以公正地评估模式。

analysis_en.main_results: El bendiocarb mostró los valores más altos de riesgo de efectos no cancerígenos sobre la salud, con HQ > 1 (riesgo alto) y incrementos significativos de 1.35, 2.7 y 4.1 conforme aumentaron los años de exposición laboral (5, 10 y 15 años, respectivamente). La bifentrina y el pirimifos metil presentaron incrementos proporcionales al tiempo de exposición laboral, pero con valores de HQ < 1 (riesgo bajo).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: Los resultados indican que el bendiocarb representa el mayor riesgo para la salud en comparación con los otros dos pesticidas, lo cual es una observación directa basada en los cálculos de riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI).
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Estos hallazgos pueden informar la necesidad de implementar medidas de protección más estrictas para los trabajadores expuestos al bendiocarb, así como guiar la selección de pesticidas en programas de control de vectores de enfermedades víricas en México.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: El estudio se basa en datos abstractos y no proporciona información detallada sobre la metodología o controles utilizados, lo que limita la confianza en los resultados. Sin embargo, los hallazgos son directos y se basan en cálculos de riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI), lo que justifica una evaluación de confianza moderada.

papers.title_zh: 估计墨西哥 媒介 控制中使用的农药和农药的健康状况
papers.source_body_en: El uso de pesticidas en México se ha promovido ampliamente para el control y combate de vectores que transmiten enfermedades víricas como chikungunya, dengue, paludismo y zika, que actualmente constituyen un problema de salud pública en el país, siendo el sector laboral dedicado a la aplicación de estos productos la población más expuesta. En el presente estudio se estimó el riesgo para la salud por exposición ocupacional a los principales pesticidas utilizados para el control de vectores de enfermedades, recomendados por el Centro Nacional de Programas Preventivos y Control de Enfermedades (CENAPRECE) y potencialmente tóxicos para los seres humanos (bifentrina, pirimifos-metil y bendiocarb). Para ello, se identificaron sus posibles efectos sobre la salud considerando su potencial tóxico (pT) y neurotóxico (pNe), así como la dosis de exposición estimada (DEE) en el ámbito laboral, de acuerdo con los años de exposición. Se determinaron el riesgo no cancerígeno individual (HQi) y el índice de riesgo (HI). Se encontró que el bendiocarb presentó los valores más altos de riesgo de efectos no cancerígenos sobre la salud (HQ > 1 = riesgo alto), con incrementos significativos de 1.35, 2.7 y 4.1 conforme aumentaron los años de exposición laboral (5, 10 y 15 años, respectivamente). Por su parte, la bifentrina y el pirimifos metil mostraron incrementos proporcionales al tiempo de exposición laboral, pero con valores de HQ < 1 (bajo riesgo). Por lo tanto, el bendiocarb es el pesticida que representa la mayor preocupación para la salud. Sin embargo, no se deben descartar los otros dos compuestos, ya que puede haber un riesgo acumulado. Esto se debe a que los tres pesticidas pueden afectar el mismo órgano o sistema de órganos.
papers.abstract_zh: 在墨西哥,杀虫剂的使用已被广泛推广,用于控制和防治通过病毒传播的疾病(如基孔肯雅热、登革热、疟疾和寨卡病毒病),这些疾病目前已成为墨西哥的公共卫生问题,而从事这些产品喷洒的劳动者则是暴露风险最高的人群。本研究估算了墨西哥国家预防与疾病控制中心(CENAPRECE)推荐用于控制上述媒介传播疾病且对人类具有潜在毒性的主要杀虫剂(联苯菊酯、甲基嘧啶磷和混灭威)的职业暴露健康风险。为此,研究识别了这些杀虫剂的潜在健康影响,包括其毒性潜力(pT)和神经毒性潜力(pNe),以及根据职业暴露年限估算的暴露剂量(DEE)。研究计算了个体非致癌风险(HQi)和风险指数(HI)。结果显示,混灭威在非致癌健康影响风险方面呈现最高值(HQ > 1 = 高风险),且随着职业暴露年限(5年、10年和15年)的增加,风险值分别显著上升至1.35、2.7和4.1。而联苯菊酯和甲基嘧啶磷则显示出与职业暴露时间成正比的风险增加,但HQ值均<1(低风险)。因此,混灭威是对健康构成最大关注的杀虫剂。然而,不应忽视其他两种化合物,因为可能存在累积风险。这是因为三种杀虫剂可能影响同一器官或系统。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 研究人员研究了墨西哥基孔肯雅热病害防治中使用 媒介 杀虫剂控制害虫的劳动问题,旨在解决公共健康问题。我们的目的是评估卫生协会在工作中使用杀虫剂的情况。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们致力于对墨西哥的 媒介 病毒防治职业病害防治状况进行评估。请考虑 CENAPRECE 推荐的主要杀虫剂,包括苯虫威、联苯三唑和吡咪磷,对人体具有潜在的毒性。
analysis_zh.methods: 识别潜在毒性 (pT) 和神经毒性 (pNe) 的害虫防治效果,并根据暴露估计剂量 (DEE) 和劳动强度,快速应对暴露情况。可以计算出没有癌症基因的个体 (HQi) 和有杀虫剂的个体 (HI)。
analysis_zh.main_results: 苯硫卡最重要的价值是无癌症的健康,与 HQ > 1 (riesgo alto) 和 1.35、2.7 和 4.1 的显着增量一致,符合劳动日的 años de exosición 劳动(分别为 5、10 和 15 年)。La bifentrina y el pirimifos metil Presentaron Incrementos Incrementos Al tiempo de exposición Laboral,pero con valores de HQ < 1 (riesgo bajo).
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 印度苯虫威的结果代表了市长对其他杀虫剂的健康比较,通过直接观察来计算没有癌症的个人 (HQi) 和国家 (HI)。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 我们将通知您对使用双效苯乙威的工人实施保护措施的必要性,并根据墨西哥 媒介 病毒控制计划选择杀虫剂。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 我们的研究涉及抽象数据,并且没有详细说明控制使用方法的比例信息,但限制了结果的机密性。禁运,我们的指导方针是对个人癌症基因计算 (HQi) 和癌症指数 (HI) 进行计算,以公正地评估模式。

Chikungunya Joint Pain: Relapse or Reinfection? by Dr. Ankita Balar Arya on Aug 15 2026 12:55 PM Chikungunya joint pain can return months after the fever is gone. But recurring pain does not necessarily mean you have caught the virus again. The fever may be gone, the rash may have disappeared and the infection may seem like a thing of the past. Then, weeks or months later, the fingers, knees or ankles begin hurting again. This can make one question whether chikungunya has returned. In most cases, recurring joint pain after chikungunya does not mean that a person has been infected again. Persistent or recurrent joint pain is a recognized long-term consequence of chikungunya, and WHO notes that joint symptoms can continue for months or even years after the initial illness. (1Chikungunya Go to source) The important distinction is between a new chikungunya infection and ongoing or recurrent joint symptoms after the first infection. Current evidence suggests that people who have recovered from chikungunya are likely to be immune to future infection, although WHO notes that research on reinfection is still ongoing. Therefore, recurring joint pain should not automatically be interpreted as proof of a second chikungunya infection. Chikungunya - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment. FAQs Chikungunya is a viral disease spread by mosquito bites; it causes fever, severe joint pain and rash on the body. Chikungunya occurs in Africa, Asia and the Indian sub continent. Chikungunya Joint Pain After Recovery: Why Can It Come Back? "A vast majority of patients coming in with secondary flare-ups months after recovering from viral fever assume they have been bitten and infected again, but true reinfection with chikungunya is extraordinarily rare due to long-lasting neutralizing antibody protection," explains Dr Rommel Tickoo, Director of Internal Medicine at Max Super Specialty Hospital. If the virus is cleared from the bloodstream, the reasons behind the joints continuing to ache can be found in peer-reviewed studies in journals like Frontiers in Immunology and Arthritis and Rheumatology that point to two main primary drivers: 1. Viral Persistence In Joint Reservoirs While the body clears the active virus from circulation within 7 to 12 days, viral RNA remnants and viral proteins can hide inside joint tissues, specifically within synovial fibroblasts and macrophages. These "viral sanctuaries" trigger localised, recurring inflammatory responses whenever the immune system detects leftover viral debris. 2. Autoimmune Mimicry And Immune Dysregulation In some individuals, the intense immune response triggered during acute chikungunya misinterprets normal joint tissue for viral invaders. Pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha) remain chronically elevated, causing the body to attack its own joint lining, giving rise to symptoms that mimic rheumatoid arthritis. New Insights on Chikungunya Virus and Chronic Joint Pain One fourth of the patients infected with chikungunya have chronic joint pain. However, the virus was not detected in the joints after 22 months of infection. Post-Chikungunya Arthritis: What Science Says About Long-Term Pain Dr Rommel Tickoo explains, "What patients actually experience is post-chikungunya chronic inflammatory arthralgia. When viral RNA fragments or immune complexes lodge in the joint synovial tissue, they trigger intermittent inflammatory waves.” He adds, "Managing this requires a structured medical approach using targeted anti-inflammatory therapy, physical rehabilitation, and monitoring by a physician or rheumatologist rather than self-medicating with over-the-counter painkillers." Research reveals that post-chikungunya joint disease follows a relapsing-remitting course rather than a continuous one for many patients: Studies published in PMC Public Health show that 10-15% of patients progress to long-term chronic joint involvement that persists for over a year post-infection, with some cohorts reporting relapsing joint pain up to 36 months later. Individuals over the age of 45, women, and those with pre-existing joint conditions (like osteoarthritis) are statistically at a higher risk of experiencing post-viral relapses. Weather shifts (especially humidity and cold temperatures), physical overexertion, mental stress, and intercurrent infections often trigger a flare-up of joint pain. Arthritis Linked to Mosquito-borne Viruses Infection induced by Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) and Ross River virus (RRV) is transmitted by mosquitoes and causes severe arthritis, muscle pain, and fever. Can Chikungunya Happen Twice? What We Know About Reinfection No. True reinfection with the chikungunya virus is extremely rare. Once you recover from a primary chikungunya infection, your immune system generates long-lasting neutralising antibodies that protect you against future infections for life. Recurring symptoms are a sign of post-viral joint inflammation (relapse), not a second infection. However, this statement is stronger than current WHO guidance. WHO states that it is unlikely that people who have been infected with chikungunya will become reinfected, while noting that research is still ongoing. WHO also explains that chronic chikungunya can manifest as joint pain lasting months or years and that this does not mean the person has been infected more than once. Quiz on Chikungunya Chikungunya is a viral disease transmitted by mosquito bite. Test your knowledge on Chikungunya by taking this quiz. ... How to Manage Recurring Chikungunya Joint Pain Managing post-chikungunya joint pain requires a multi-pronged approach under clinical supervision: Medication: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or short-term disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) prescribed by a rheumatologist for severe flares. Low-Impact Movement: Hydrotherapy, light stretching, and gentler physical exercise to maintain joint mobility without triggering mechanical inflammation. Anti-Inflammatory Care: Warm compresses for morning stiffness, combined with an anti-inflammatory diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids and antioxidants. Importantly, WHO advises that NSAIDs such as ibuprofen should be avoided until dengue has been ruled out, because they can increase bleeding risk in people with dengue. Management of chikungunya is primarily focused on relieving symptoms, maintaining hydration and supporting recovery. When Should You See a Rheumatologist for Chikungunya Pain? You should consult a specialist if your joint pain persists beyond 4 to 6 weeks post-recovery, if you notice visible joint swelling, redness, or heat, or if morning stiffness lasts longer than 45 minutes and severely impacts mobility. Persistent joint symptoms deserve medical attention because chronic chikungunya-related musculoskeletal problems can resemble other inflammatory joint conditions. A clinician can assess the symptoms and determine whether further evaluation or specialist management is appropriate. Living with post-chikungunya arthralgia can feel discouraging, especially when a flare-up strikes out of nowhere. Remind yourself that a relapse does not mean you are sick with a fresh infection or contagious to those around you. By working closely with a rheumatologist, pacing your daily activities, and protecting your joints from overexertion, you can manage the inflammatory cycles while your immune system gradually restores balance. For many people, the return of joint pain after chikungunya can be frightening, but it does not automatically mean the virus has come back. Understanding that chikungunya joint pain can persist long after the initial infection can help separate a lingering recovery problem from a suspected new infection. With appropriate medical evaluation and supportive care, patients can better understand their symptoms and take informed steps toward recovery. Chikungunya Joint Pain: Relapse or Reinfection? by Dr. Ankita Balar Arya on Aug 15 2026 12:55 PM Chikungunya joint pain can return months after the fever is gone. But recurring pain does not necessarily mean you have caught the virus again. The fever may be gone, the rash may have disappeared and the infection may seem like a thing of the past. Then, weeks or months later, the fingers, knees or ankles begin hurting again. This can make one question whether chikungunya has returned. In most cases, recurring joint pain after chikungunya does not mean that a person has been infected again. Persistent or recurrent joint pain is a recognized long-term consequence of chikungunya, and WHO notes that joint symptoms can continue for months or even years after the initial illness. (1Chikungunya Go to source) The important distinction is between a new chikungunya infection and ongoing or recurrent joint symptoms after the first infection. Current evidence suggests that people who have recovered from chikungunya are likely to be immune to future infection, although WHO notes that research on reinfection is still ongoing. Therefore, recurring joint pain should not automatically be interpreted as proof of a second chikungunya infection. Chikungunya - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment. FAQs Chikungunya is a viral disease spread by mosquito bites; it causes fever, severe joint pain and rash on the body. Chikungunya occurs in Africa, Asia and the Indian sub continent. Chikungunya Joint Pain After Recovery: Why Can It Come Back? "A vast majority of patients coming in with secondary flare-ups months after recovering from viral fever assume they have been bitten and infected again, but true reinfection with chikungunya is extraordinarily rare due to long-lasting neutralizing antibody protection," explains Dr Rommel Tickoo, Director of Internal Medicine at Max Super Specialty Hospital. If the virus is cleared from the bloodstream, the reasons behind the joints continuing to ache can be found in peer-reviewed studies in journals like Frontiers in Immunology and Arthritis and Rheumatology that point to two main primary drivers: 1. Viral Persistence In Joint Reservoirs While the body clears the active virus from circulation within 7 to 12 days, viral RNA remnants and viral proteins can hide inside joint tissues, specifically within synovial fibroblasts and macrophages. These "viral sanctuaries" trigger localised, recurring inflammatory responses whenever the immune system detects leftover viral debris. 2. Autoimmune Mimicry And Immune Dysregulation In some individuals, the intense immune response triggered during acute chikungunya misinterprets normal joint tissue for viral invaders. Pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha) remain chronically elevated, causing the body to attack its own joint lining, giving rise to symptoms that mimic rheumatoid arthritis. New Insights on Chikungunya Virus and Chronic Joint Pain One fourth of the patients infected with chikungunya have chronic joint pain. However, the virus was not detected in the joints after 22 months of infection. Post-Chikungunya Arthritis: What Science Says About Long-Term Pain Dr Rommel Tickoo explains, "What patients actually experience is post-chikungunya chronic inflammatory arthralgia. When viral RNA fragments or immune complexes lodge in the joint synovial tissue, they trigger intermittent inflammatory waves.” He adds, "Managing this requires a structured medical approach using targeted anti-inflammatory therapy, physical rehabilitation, and monitoring by a physician or rheumatologist rather than self-medicating with over-the-counter painkillers." Research reveals that post-chikungunya joint disease follows a relapsing-remitting course rather than a continuous one for many patients: Studies published in PMC Public Health show that 10-15% of patients progress to long-term chronic joint involvement that persists for over a year post-infection, with some cohorts reporting relapsing joint pain up to 36 months later. Individuals over the age of 45, women, and those with pre-existing joint conditions (like osteoarthritis) are statistically at a higher risk of experiencing post-viral relapses. Weather shifts (especially humidity and cold temperatures), physical overexertion, mental stress, and intercurrent infections often trigger a flare-up of joint pain. Arthritis Linked to Mosquito-borne Viruses Infection induced by Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) and Ross River virus (RRV) is transmitted by mosquitoes and causes severe arthritis, muscle pain, and fever. Can Chikungunya Happen Twice? What We Know About Reinfection No. True reinfection with the chikungunya virus is extremely rare. Once you recover from a primary chikungunya infection, your immune system generates long-lasting neutralising antibodies that protect you against future infections for life. Recurring symptoms are a sign of post-viral joint inflammation (relapse), not a second infection. However, this statement is stronger than current WHO guidance. WHO states that it is unlikely that people who have been infected with chikungunya will become reinfected, while noting that research is still ongoing. WHO also explains that chronic chikungunya can manifest as joint pain lasting months or years and that this does not mean the person has been infected more than once. Quiz on Chikungunya Chikungunya is a viral disease transmitted by mosquito bite. Test your knowledge on Chikungunya by taking this quiz. ... How to Manage Recurring Chikungunya Joint Pain Managing post-chikungunya joint pain requires a multi-pronged approach under clinical supervision: Medication: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or short-term disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) prescribed by a rheumatologist for severe flares. Low-Impact Movement: Hydrotherapy, light stretching, and gentler physical exercise to maintain joint mobility without triggering mechanical inflammation. Anti-Inflammatory Care: Warm compresses for morning stiffness, combined with an anti-inflammatory diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids and antioxidants. Importantly, WHO advises that NSAIDs such as ibuprofen should be avoided until dengue has been ruled out, because they can increase bleeding risk in people with dengue. Management of chikungunya is primarily focused on relieving symptoms, maintaining hydration and supporting recovery. When Should You See a Rheumatologist for Chikungunya Pain? You should consult a specialist if your joint pain persists beyond 4 to 6 weeks post-recovery, if you notice visible joint swelling, redness, or heat, or if morning stiffness lasts longer than 45 minutes and severely impacts mobility. Persistent joint symptoms deserve medical attention because chronic chikungunya-related musculoskeletal problems can resemble other inflammatory joint conditions. A clinician can assess the symptoms and determine whether further evaluation or specialist management is appropriate. Living with post-chikungunya arthralgia can feel discouraging, especially when a flare-up strikes out of nowhere. Remind yourself that a relapse does not mean you are sick with a fresh infection or contagious to those around you. By working closely with a rheumatologist, pacing your daily activities, and protecting your joints from overexertion, you can manage the inflammatory cycles while your immune system gradually restores balance. For many people, the return of joint pain after chikungunya can be frightening, but it does not automatically mean the virus has come back. Understanding that chikungunya joint pain can persist long after the initial infection can help separate a lingering recovery problem from a suspected new infection. With appropriate medical evaluation and supportive care, patients can better understand their symptoms and take informed steps toward recovery. analysis.brief_en: Post‐chikungunya joint pain, often described as a relapse, can reappear months after the acute fever has resolved. A Medindia report by Ankita Balar Arya (Aug 15 2026) notes that the pain may affect fingers, knees or ankles and can be mistaken for a new infection, though true reinfection with chikungunya is extremely rare. WHO states that long‐lasting neutralizing antibodies usually protect against future infection, while research on reinfection remains ongoing. Approximately one‐quarter of chikungunya patients develop chronic joint pain, and 10‐15 % experience persistent arthralgia for more than a year, with risk heightened in individuals over 45, women, and those with pre‐existing joint disease. Flare‐ups may be triggered by weather changes, physical strain, stress or intercurrent infections. Management includes NSAIDs (avoided until dengue is excluded), NSAID‐sparing DMARDs, physiotherapy, warm compresses, and anti‐inflammatory dietary measures, with specialist rheumatology referral advised if pain persists beyond 4‐6 weeks or is accompanied by swelling, redness, or prolonged morning stiffness.

news.content_zh: 基孔肯雅热后关节疼痛通常被描述为复发,可能在急性发烧消退几个月后再次出现。Ankita Balar Arya 的 Medindia 报告(2026 年 8 月 15 日)指出,疼痛可能会影响手指、膝盖或脚踝,并可能被误认为是新的感染,尽管真正的基孔肯雅热再次感染极为罕见。世界卫生组织指出,持久的中和抗体通常可以防止未来的感染,而关于再次感染的研究仍在进行中。大约四分之一的基孔肯雅热患者会出现慢性关节疼痛,10-15% 的患者会经历持续一年以上的 关节痛,其中 45 岁以上的个体、女性和已有关节疾病的患者风险更高。天气变化、身体劳损、压力或并发感染可能会引发疾病发作。治疗方法包括使用 NSAID(在排除登革热之前避免使用)、保留 NSAID 的 DMARD、物理治疗、热敷和抗炎饮食措施,如果疼痛持续超过 4-6 周或伴有肿胀、发红或长时间晨僵,建议转诊风湿病专家。

news.content_zh: 据报道,印度喀拉拉邦瓦蒂约卡武市基孔肯雅热病例激增,促使卫生部门召开特别审查会议来解决这一问题。暴发 引起了批评,居民声称没有采取足够的措施来防止积水和控制蚊蝇数量。瓦蒂约卡武 (Vattiyoorkavu) 内的瓦兹图科南 (Vazhottukonam) 基孔肯雅热病例数量相对较多,还有报道称该地区登革热和病毒热病例不断增加。为此,卫生部门决定加强针对特定地区的干预措施,以遏制这些疾病的传播。尽管卫生官员声称定期采取预防措施,但情况仍未得到解决,报告的病例数量也没有减少。这次会议由地区医疗官员主持,此前马诺拉马发表了一份关于基孔肯雅热在该地区持续蔓延的报告。

analysis_zh.time: 2026 年 8 月 14 日,据报道瓦蒂约卡武 (Vattiyoorkavu) 基孔肯雅热病例激增,卫生部门于周四召开了一次特别审查会议(日期未具体说明,但很可能在同一时间范围内)。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 暴发 疫情发生在印度喀拉拉邦瓦蒂约卡武 (Vattiyoorkavu) 地区,特别关注瓦兹图科南 (Vazhottukonam),该地区基孔肯雅热病例 发病率 数量较多。
analysis_zh.event: 瓦蒂约卡武的卫生当局因未能充分控制基孔肯雅热病例激增而面临批评,卫生部门召开了特别审查会议以实施强化干预措施。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: Vazhottukonam 报告的基孔肯雅热病例数量相对较高,Vattiyoorkavu 地区的登革热和病毒热病例也有所增加。卫生部门已决定加强针对特定地区的干预措施,以遏制传播。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 卫生部门已召开特别审查会议,正在实施针对特定地区的强化干预措施,以遏制基孔肯雅热、登革热和病毒热的传播。然而,当地居民表示,预防措施并未得到充分落实。

news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：2026 年 8 月 14 日，据报道瓦蒂约卡武 (Vattiyoorkavu) 基孔肯雅热病例激增，卫生部门于周四召开了一次特...；地点与对象：暴发 疫情发生在印度喀拉拉邦瓦蒂约卡武 (Vattiyoorkavu) 地区，特别关注瓦兹图科南 (Vazhottukonam)，该地区基孔肯雅热病例 发病率 数量较多。；事件：瓦蒂约卡武的卫生当局因未能充分控制基孔肯雅热病例激增而面临批评，卫生部门召开了特别审查会议以实施强化干预措施。；影响与风险：Vazhottukonam 报告的基孔肯雅热病例数量相对较高，Vattiyoorkavu 地区的登革热和病毒热病例也有所增加。卫生部门已决定加强针对特定地区的干预措施，以遏制传播。；应对与不确定性：卫生部门已召开特别审查会议，正在实施针对特定地区的强化干预措施，以遏制基孔肯雅热、登革热和病毒热的传播。然而，当地居民表示，预防措施并未得到充分落实。

news.content_title: Chikungunya joint pain months later: relapse or reinfection?
news.content: Image: Web New Delhi: Chikungunya is often associated with sudden fever, rash and severe joint pain, but for some people, the discomfort does not end when the initial infection clears. Stiff fingers, aching knees, swollen joints and ankle pain can return weeks or months after the acute illness, leaving recovered patients wondering whether they have contracted the mosquito-borne viral infection again. Infectious Diseases In most cases, recurring joint symptoms after chikungunya are not evidence of reinfection . They can instead be linked to prolonged inflammation following the original infection, commonly described as post-chikungunya chronic inflammatory arthralgia or arthritis. Understanding the difference between a new infection and lingering post-viral joint inflammation can help patients avoid unnecessary anxiety and seek appropriate medical care. Reinfection and relapse are different Chikungunya is caused by the chikungunya virus (CHIKV), which is transmitted primarily through infected Aedes mosquitoes. During the acute phase, patients commonly experience high fever, intense joint pain, muscle pain, headache and sometimes a rash. Although the fever and other symptoms generally improve, joint problems can persist in some patients. A reinfection would mean contracting chikungunya again after recovering from an earlier infection. This is considered uncommon because infection generally produces a strong immune response and neutralising antibodies. A relapse or post-viral flare , on the other hand, refers to the recurrence or persistence of joint symptoms after the acute infection has subsided. Therefore, someone who develops joint stiffness several months after chikungunya should not automatically assume that they have been bitten by an infected mosquito again. Why can joint pain continue? The chikungunya virus is particularly notable for its effect on the joints. Arthritis During the acute infection, the body’s immune response produces inflammation that contributes substantially to the severe joint pain experienced by patients. In some individuals, this inflammatory process does not completely settle after the initial illness. Research has suggested that viral material and immune responses within joint tissues may contribute to prolonged inflammation. Some studies have investigated the presence of viral RNA or viral proteins in tissues and the role of immune cells in maintaining inflammation. However, the exact mechanisms behind persistent chikungunya arthritis are complex and are still being studied. This means that recurring pain should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence that a complete new viral infection has begun. The role of the immune system One important explanation for prolonged symptoms is continued immune activation. During chikungunya infection, the immune system releases inflammatory signalling molecules to fight the virus. In some patients, inflammation can continue after the acute phase. This can produce symptoms resembling inflammatory arthritis, including morning stiffness, swelling and difficulty moving affected joints. Substance Abuse The severity and duration of symptoms can vary considerably between individuals. Some people recover completely within a relatively short period, while others experience intermittent joint pain for many months. Not everyone experiences the same symptoms Post-chikungunya joint problems can affect different parts of the body. Commonly affected areas include: Fingers and hands Wrists Knees Ankles Feet Elbows Patients may experience stiffness after waking up, pain while walking or difficulty performing everyday activities involving the hands. Symptoms can also follow a relapsing and remitting pattern , meaning that a person may feel significantly better for a period before experiencing another flare. Anatomy This unpredictable pattern can make patients believe that the infection has returned. Why symptoms may fluctuate Post-viral joint inflammation does not necessarily remain constant. Physical overexertion can aggravate already inflamed joints. Changes in weather, stress and other illnesses may also coincide with worsening symptoms in some people. However, individual triggers vary, and not every episode of pain after chikungunya is necessarily caused by the original infection. Persistent or recurring joint symptoms should therefore be assessed rather than automatically attributed to chikungunya. Who may be more vulnerable? Research has found that certain groups may have a greater risk of developing prolonged joint problems after chikungunya. Older adults and people who already have joint-related conditions may be more vulnerable to persistent symptoms. Some studies have also reported differences according to sex and other individual factors. The course of the illness can also depend on the severity of the initial infection and the person’s overall health. Importantly, experiencing prolonged joint pain does not mean that every patient will develop permanent arthritis. Health Conditions Can chikungunya be contracted twice? True repeat infection with chikungunya appears to be very uncommon , largely because recovery generally produces a strong immune response. However, the statement that reinfection is absolutely impossible should be avoided. Evidence regarding the duration and completeness of immunity continues to be studied, and individual circumstances can differ. For someone who has previously recovered from chikungunya and later develops joint pain, a post-chikungunya inflammatory condition is generally a more plausible explanation than assuming a second infection. A doctor may consider other causes as well, particularly if symptoms are new, severe or accompanied by fever. When should medical attention be sought? Persistent joint pain should not simply be ignored, especially when it interferes with normal activities. Medical evaluation is advisable when symptoms continue for several weeks after the initial infection or repeatedly return. People should particularly seek medical advice if they develop: Persistent or significant joint swelling Redness or warmth around a joint Severe or worsening pain Prolonged morning stiffness Difficulty walking or using the hands Recurrent fever Symptoms that interfere with work or daily activities A physician may determine whether the symptoms are consistent with post-chikungunya arthritis or whether another condition needs to be investigated. Infectious Diseases Treatment depends on the individual There is no single treatment that works for everyone with prolonged chikungunya-related joint symptoms. Doctors may recommend appropriate pain-relieving or anti-inflammatory medicines depending on the patient’s symptoms, medical history and other risk factors. In more persistent inflammatory arthritis, a rheumatologist may consider additional treatments, including disease-modifying medicines. Patients should not start prescription medicines, including corticosteroids or disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs, without medical supervision. The treatment approach may also change depending on whether the patient is still experiencing an acute infection or is dealing with post-viral inflammatory disease. Movement and rehabilitation can help Physical activity is another important component of recovery. Complete inactivity may lead to stiffness and loss of muscle strength, while excessive exercise can aggravate painful joints. Gentle stretching, mobility exercises, walking and other low-impact activities may help maintain joint function. Physiotherapy can be particularly useful for people who continue to experience significant stiffness or difficulty with movement. Arthritis The appropriate level of exercise should depend on the severity of symptoms, and patients experiencing substantial inflammation should seek professional advice before beginning an intensive exercise programme. Self-medication can be risky People recovering from chikungunya sometimes rely heavily on over-the-counter painkillers when symptoms return. However, taking medicines repeatedly without medical advice can cause complications, particularly in people with kidney disease, stomach problems, cardiovascular conditions or other health issues. It is also important not to assume that every episode of fever and joint pain after chikungunya is automatically a relapse. Other infections and inflammatory conditions can produce similar symptoms. A fresh fever may warrant medical assessment, particularly in areas where mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue and chikungunya circulate. Prevention remains important Even though post-chikungunya joint pain is generally not the result of a new infection, mosquito-bite prevention remains important. Removing stagnant water around homes, using mosquito repellents, wearing clothing that reduces exposed skin and maintaining appropriate mosquito-control measures can help reduce the risk of chikungunya and other mosquito-borne infections. Community-level control of mosquito breeding sites is equally important during periods of increased mosquito activity. Substance Abuse Conclusion Joint pain returning months after chikungunya can be frightening, but it does not automatically mean that the virus has infected the person again. For many survivors, persistent or recurring pain is associated with post-chikungunya inflammatory joint disease rather than a fresh infection. The condition can fluctuate and, in some cases, continue for an extended period. Anyone experiencing prolonged swelling, severe pain, significant morning stiffness or difficulty with everyday movement should consult a doctor, and persistent inflammatory symptoms may require evaluation by a rheumatologist. With appropriate medical assessment, physical rehabilitation and individually tailored treatment, many patients can manage these recurring symptoms and gradually regain mobility. However, individual triggers vary, and not every episode of pain after chikungunya is necessarily caused by the original infection. Persistent or recurring joint symptoms should therefore be assessed rather than automatically attributed to chikungunya. Who may be more vulnerable? Research has found that certain groups may have a greater risk of developing prolonged joint problems after chikungunya. Older adults and people who already have joint-related conditions may be more vulnerable to persistent symptoms. Some studies have also reported differences according to sex and other individual factors. The course of the illness can also depend on the severity of the initial infection and the person’s overall health. Importantly, experiencing prolonged joint pain does not mean that every patient will develop permanent arthritis. Health Conditions Can chikungunya be contracted twice? True repeat infection with chikungunya appears to be very uncommon , largely because recovery generally produces a strong immune response. However, the statement that reinfection is absolutely impossible should be avoided. Evidence regarding the duration and completeness of immunity continues to be studied, and individual circumstances can differ. For someone who has previously recovered from chikungunya and later develops joint pain, a post-chikungunya inflammatory condition is generally a more plausible explanation than assuming a second infection. A doctor may consider other causes as well, particularly if symptoms are new, severe or accompanied by fever. When should medical attention be sought? Persistent joint pain should not simply be ignored, especially when it interferes with normal activities. Medical evaluation is advisable when symptoms continue for several weeks after the initial infection or repeatedly return. People should particularly seek medical advice if they develop: Persistent or significant joint swelling Redness or warmth around a joint Severe or worsening pain Prolonged morning stiffness Difficulty walking or using the hands Recurrent fever Symptoms that interfere with work or daily activities A physician may determine whether the symptoms are consistent with post-chikungunya arthritis or whether another condition needs to be investigated. Infectious Diseases Treatment depends on the individual There is no single treatment that works for everyone with prolonged chikungunya-related joint symptoms. Doctors may recommend appropriate pain-relieving or anti-inflammatory medicines depending on the patient’s symptoms, medical history and other risk factors. In more persistent inflammatory arthritis, a rheumatologist may consider additional treatments, including disease-modifying medicines. Patients should not start prescription medicines, including corticosteroids or disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs, without medical supervision. The treatment approach may also change depending on whether the patient is still experiencing an acute infection or is dealing with post-viral inflammatory disease. Movement and rehabilitation can help Physical activity is another important component of recovery. Complete inactivity may lead to stiffness and loss of muscle strength, while excessive exercise can aggravate painful joints. Gentle stretching, mobility exercises, walking and other low-impact activities may help maintain joint function. Physiotherapy can be particularly useful for people who continue to experience significant stiffness or difficulty with movement. Arthritis The appropriate level of exercise should depend on the severity of symptoms, and patients experiencing substantial inflammation should seek professional advice before beginning an intensive exercise programme. Self-medication can be risky People recovering from chikungunya sometimes rely heavily on over-the-counter painkillers when symptoms return. However, taking medicines repeatedly without medical advice can cause complications, particularly in people with kidney disease, stomach problems, cardiovascular conditions or other health issues. It is also important not to assume that every episode of fever and joint pain after chikungunya is automatically a relapse. Other infections and inflammatory conditions can produce similar symptoms. A fresh fever may warrant medical assessment, particularly in areas where mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue and chikungunya circulate. Prevention remains important Even though post-chikungunya joint pain is generally not the result of a new infection, mosquito-bite prevention remains important. Removing stagnant water around homes, using mosquito repellents, wearing clothing that reduces exposed skin and maintaining appropriate mosquito-control measures can help reduce the risk of chikungunya and other mosquito-borne infections. Community-level control of mosquito breeding sites is equally important during periods of increased mosquito activity. Substance Abuse Conclusion Joint pain returning months after chikungunya can be frightening, but it does not automatically mean that the virus has infected the person again. For many survivors, persistent or recurring pain is associated with post-chikungunya inflammatory joint disease rather than a fresh infection. The condition can fluctuate and, in some cases, continue for an extended period. Anyone experiencing prolonged swelling, severe pain, significant morning stiffness or difficulty with everyday movement should consult a doctor, and persistent inflammatory symptoms may require evaluation by a rheumatologist. With appropriate medical assessment, physical rehabilitation and individually tailored treatment, many patients can manage these recurring symptoms and gradually regain mobility. news.content: Image: Web New Delhi: Chikungunya is best known for causing sudden fever and severe joint pain, but for some patients, the symptoms can continue even after the acute infection has settled. Joint stiffness, swelling and musculoskeletal pain may persist for weeks or months, affecting mobility and everyday activities. Infectious Diseases During recovery, medical treatment and appropriate physical activity remain important. Diet can also support overall recovery by providing adequate protein, fluids, vitamins, minerals and healthy fats. However, no specific food or diet has been proven to cure post-chikungunya arthritis or dramatically shorten its duration. The condition develops partly because the body’s inflammatory response can continue after the acute viral illness has passed. As a result, patients may continue to experience stiffness, tenderness, swelling and difficulty moving affected joints. However, a diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy sources of protein can provide nutrients required for normal immune function and tissue repair. Dr Priyanka Rohatgi, Chief Clinical Dietitian and Executive Director of Clinical Nutrition and Dietetics at Apollo Hospitals, Bengaluru, has highlighted turmeric and curcumin as potentially useful components of a balanced recovery diet. Curcumin is a compound found in turmeric that has demonstrated anti-inflammatory properties in laboratory and clinical research. Its absorption from the digestive tract is relatively low, and black pepper contains piperine, which can increase curcumin absorption. However, turmeric should be considered a dietary ingredient rather than a substitute for prescribed medicines. 1. Include turmeric and other polyphenol-rich foods Turmeric can be incorporated into ordinary meals, soups or milk-based beverages. Combining turmeric with black pepper is commonly suggested because piperine can improve the absorption of curcumin. Adding a small amount of healthy fat to a meal may also help with the absorption of fat-soluble compounds. Other foods containing potentially beneficial plant compounds include berries, colourful vegetables, leafy greens, ginger, garlic, green tea and a variety of fruits. Rather than relying on one so-called “superfood”, patients can benefit from consuming a wide variety of plant foods throughout the week. Health Conditions 2. Add sources of omega-3 fats Omega-3 fatty acids are another important component of a balanced diet. Fatty fish such as sardines, mackerel and salmon provide the long-chain omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA. For vegetarians, flaxseeds, chia seeds and walnuts provide alpha-linolenic acid (ALA). These foods can be included regularly as part of an overall healthy eating pattern. For example, ground flaxseed can be added to porridge or yoghurt, while soaked chia seeds can be included in a breakfast bowl or smoothie. People who eat fish can include appropriately prepared oily fish as part of their regular meals. 3. Coconut water, soups and other fluids can also contribute to daily fluid intake. Dehydration can contribute to feelings of fatigue and may make an already uncomfortable recovery period more difficult. Nutrition Fenugreek water is sometimes promoted for inflammation, but there is limited evidence that it specifically treats post-chikungunya joint pain. It should therefore not be considered essential. Breakfast Vegetable oats, vegetable upma, moong dal chilla or a balanced breakfast containing whole grains and protein can provide sustained energy. Adding spinach or other vegetables increases the meal’s fibre and micronutrient content. Mid-morning Fresh fruit, coconut water or plain yoghurt can provide fluids and nutrients. Amla or other vitamin C-rich fruits can also be included as part of the diet. Lunch A balanced lunch could include brown rice, millet or jowar roti, along with dal, vegetables and a source of protein. For non-vegetarians, grilled or steamed fish can be included. Vegetarians can choose dal, beans, tofu, paneer or other protein-rich foods. Health Ginger contains bioactive compounds such as gingerols, although evidence that consuming ginger specifically treats post-chikungunya arthritis remains limited. Dinner A lighter meal consisting of vegetable soup, dal, tofu or paneer and cooked vegetables can provide protein and micronutrients without being excessively heavy. Bedtime Warm milk with a small amount of turmeric can be consumed if the person tolerates dairy. A pinch of black pepper can be added, although this should be viewed as a dietary option rather than a medical treatment for joint inflammation. Excessive salt intake may also contribute to fluid retention in some people. Infectious Diseases This does not mean that patients need to follow an extremely restrictive diet. An occasional treat is unlikely to determine the course of recovery. The overall dietary pattern is more important. Protein is important for recovery Adequate protein should not be overlooked while focusing on anti-inflammatory foods. The body requires protein for maintaining muscles and supporting tissue repair. Prolonged illness and reduced physical activity can also contribute to muscle loss. Good options include dal, beans, chickpeas, eggs, fish, chicken, milk, curd, paneer, tofu, nuts and seeds. The appropriate amount depends on a person’s age, body weight, activity level and medical conditions. Gentle movement also matters Nutrition is only one component of recovery. Patients with persistent joint pain may benefit from appropriate stretching and gentle mobility exercises. However, exercise intensity should be adjusted according to symptoms. Trying to push through severe joint pain can potentially worsen discomfort. A doctor or physiotherapist can recommend an appropriate rehabilitation programme when symptoms persist. Patients experiencing prolonged swelling, significant stiffness or reduced mobility should also be evaluated by a healthcare professional to determine whether they have developed chronic chikungunya-related arthritis or another joint condition. Medical evaluation is particularly important when joint swelling or pain continues for several weeks, symptoms are worsening, movement is significantly restricted, or new symptoms develop. A doctor may assess the joints and determine whether further investigations or treatment are required. There is currently no food that can eliminate chikungunya virus-related arthritis. Dietary changes should therefore complement, rather than replace, medical care. A balanced diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, adequate protein and healthy fats can support overall recovery. Staying hydrated and limiting highly processed foods can further contribute to good nutrition. Turmeric, ginger, omega-3-rich foods and antioxidant-containing fruits and vegetables can all have a place in such a diet, but their benefits should not be overstated. For people whose joint pain persists beyond the acute infection, the most effective approach is likely to combine medical assessment, appropriate physical rehabilitation, adequate nutrition and patience as the body recovers. Understanding co-exposure to malaria and other mosquito-borne diseases Published: 08/14/2026 By Jamie Hansen, Global Health Communications Manager As the risk of several mosquito-borne diseases increases in Sub-Saharan Africa, it is critical to understand key risk factors for each disease, in addition to how they interact with one another, in order to inform local prevention strategies and policies. A new study by a team of Stanford researchers and their Kenyan colleagues, published recently in Nature Scientific Reports, sheds light on the magnitude of lifetime and recent co-exposure (being exposed to two or more of them at once) to three disease of high concern: malaria, dengue virus and chikungunya virus. They also investgiated the risk factors associated with co-exposure to these infections. Researchers followed 4,534 participants of varied ages in two urban settings in Kenya for 27 months. They found no evidence of acute infection with more than one disease at a time. However, participants showed a risk of contracting two or more of the illnesses over their lifetime ranging between 0.75-9%. Just under 9 % of participants had suffered prior dengue and chikungunya infections in their lifetimes, and just under 1% were sickened with one of these illnesses during the study. The researchers found that key risk factors included crowded homes and water collection containers near the home (which can serve as mosquito breeding grounds). These findings are important because, while malaria remains a more common disease risk in these communities, with 15.5 percent of participants testing positive, dengue and chikungunya are also significant threats and are often under-diagnosed. Additionally, they are caused by a different mosquito species with different breeding and biting patterns, which requires distinct preventive strategies from malaria. “The similar initial symptoms for all three infections complicate clinicians’ ability to identify cases of co-infection and co-exposure, which underscores the need for additional laboratory diagnostics,” said Amna Tariq, MPH, PhD, the study’s lead author and a Global Health Emerging Scholar supported by the Stanford Center for Innovation in Global Health. “Understanding the burden of co-exposure and the co-circulating burden of these diseases can help local policymakers strategize control policies such as providing mosquito nets, applying mosquito repellents, and draining water containers during peak transmission seasons.” Desiree LaBeaud, MD, MS, associate dean of the Stanford Center for Innovation in Global Health, was senior author

analysis.brief_en: A new study by Stanford researchers and their Kenyan colleagues, published in Nature Scientific Reports, investigated co-exposure to malaria, dengue virus, and chikungunya virus in two urban settings in Kenya. The research followed 4,534 participants over 27 months and found no evidence of acute co-infection with more than one disease at a time. However, participants showed a lifetime co-exposure risk ranging from 0.75-9%, with just under 9% having prior dengue and chikungunya infections. Malaria remained the most common disease, with 15.5% of participants testing positive. It also identified key risk factors, including crowded homes and water containers near residences, which serve as mosquito breeding grounds. The findings aim to inform local policymakers in developing effective control measures.

news.title_zh: 了解疟疾和其他蚊媒疾病的共同暴露 - 斯坦福大学
news.source_body_en: A new study by Stanford researchers and their Kenyan colleagues, published in Nature Scientific Reports, investigated co-exposure to malaria, dengue virus, and chikungunya virus in two urban settings in Kenya. The research followed 4,534 participants over 27 months and found no evidence of acute co-infection with more than one disease at a time. However, participants showed a lifetime co-exposure risk ranging from 0.75-9%, with just under 9% having prior dengue and chikungunya infections. Malaria remained the most common disease, with 15.5% of participants testing positive. The study highlighted the importance of understanding co-exposure dynamics, as the similar initial symptoms of these diseases complicate diagnosis. It also identified key risk factors, including crowded homes and water containers near residences, which serve as mosquito breeding grounds. The researchers called for improved laboratory diagnostics and emphasized the need for tailored prevention strategies, as these diseases are caused by different mosquito species and require distinct interventions. The findings aim to inform local policymakers in developing effective control measures.
news.content_zh: 斯坦福大学研究人员和他们的肯尼亚同事发表在《自然科学报告》上的一项新研究调查了肯尼亚两个城市环境中疟疾、登革热病毒和 基孔肯雅病毒 的共同暴露情况。该研究对 4,534 名参与者进行了 27 个月的跟踪调查,没有发现同时感染超过一种疾病的急性合并感染的证据。然而,参与者的终生共同暴露风险为 0.75-9%,其中略低于 9% 的人曾感染过登革热和基孔肯雅热。疟疾仍然是最常见的疾病,15.5% 的参与者检测呈阳性。该研究强调了了解共同暴露动态的重要性,因为这些疾病的相似初始症状使 诊断 变得复杂。它还确定了关键的风险因素,包括拥挤的房屋和住宅附近的水容器,这些都是蚊子的滋生地。研究人员呼吁改进实验室诊断,并强调需要制定量身定制的预防策略,因为这些疾病是由不同的蚊子种类引起的,需要不同的干预措施。研究结果旨在为当地政策制定者制定有效的控制措施提供信息。

news.content: Home News Obituary Recipes Charity Special ಕನ್ನಡ Live TV RADIO Advertise Contact Us Matrimonial Properties Jobs General Ads Red Chillies Music Ask Dr Greetings Astrology Tribute Of Love Latest Childhood malnutrition threatens Pakistan’s economic future Mon, Aug 17 Think twice before taking antibiotics for monsoon fever Mon, Aug 17 Diet soda may be better than fruit juice for liver health: Expert Mon, Aug 17 Most children labelled beta-lactam allergic may not be truly allergic Mon, Aug 17 Blood pressure drug may slow rare brain disease in children: Study Sun, Aug 16 1 Gujarat expands ESIC network with six more healthcare institutions Sun, Aug 16 Dengue cases rise among children in Chengalpattu Sun, Aug 16 Health Think twice before taking antibiotics for monsoon fever Mon, Aug 17 2026 03:38:50 PM Daijiworld Media Network - New Delhi New Delhi, Aug 17: The rainy season often brings a familiar medical routine — someone develops a fever, someone recommends an antibiotic and within hours a strip of tablets appears on the kitchen counter. Doctors, however, warn that this seemingly harmless practice can backfire. Monsoon fevers can be caused by several infections, including dengue, chikungunya, malaria, typhoid, influenza and leptospirosis. Antibiotics, however, do not work against all of these infections. Taking them when they are not required can also contribute to antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Dr Prerna Goyal, Senior Consultant - Physician at RG Hospitals, Ludhiana, said monsoon brings a predictable rise in different types of fever, but many people automatically turn to antibiotics. “Most monsoon fevers are viral. Dengue and chikungunya, for example, are mosquito-borne viral infections. Antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses. So taking an antibiotic for dengue or chikungunya does nothing to treat the virus causing the illness,” she said. Self-medication with antibiotics is common during the monsoon, Dr Goyal said. Some patients reach doctors after taking antibiotics on their own for a week. In such cases, doctors have to deal not only with the original illness but also with the effects of medicines that may not have been necessary. Dengue and chikungunya are mosquito-borne viral infections and do not have a bacterial component that antibiotics can target. Therefore, a person who develops fever along with symptoms such as a rash or joint pain should not automatically take an antibiotic. Such symptoms may require appropriate testing for dengue or chikungunya. Doctors say identifying the cause of the fever should come before deciding on treatment. Not every monsoon fever is viral. Some infections, including typhoid, are bacterial and may require antibiotics. However, this does not mean that patients should select an antibiotic from their medicine cabinet. Dr Goyal pointed out that prescribing the wrong antibiotic, or starting the right antibiotic too early before a proper diagnosis, can mask symptoms, make accurate testing more difficult and contribute to antimicrobial resistance. Even when an antibiotic is eventually required, guessing which medicine to take is not the same as treating the infection correctly. Dr Niraj Kumar, Senior Consultant, Internal Medicine, ShardaCare - HealthCity, said many people believe antibiotics will make a monsoon fever disappear faster. “When the fever is caused by a virus, an antibiotic does not help. Unnecessary medicines can also cause side effects and contribute to antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This happens when bacteria gradually become resistant to medicines designed to kill them or stop their growth,” he said. Antimicrobial resistance can make infections that were once relatively easy to treat much harder to manage in the future. Doctors advise that the first response to a fever should not necessarily be reaching for an antibiotic. Patients should observe their symptoms, rest, stay properly hydrated and monitor their condition, particularly when a viral illness is suspected. Dr Goyal recommends medical evaluation if fever persists for more than two to three days, with blood tests considered before medication is started when appropriate. Fever accompanied by a rash or significant joint pain may require testing for dengue or chikungunya. Other symptoms and the patient's medical history can help doctors identify other possible causes. Dr Kumar also advises people to seek medical attention promptly if fever persists or warning symptoms develop. Any fever lasting more than 48 to 72 hours, particularly if it is not improving or is accompanied by other concerning symptoms, warrants medical evaluation. Doctors emphasise that the biggest mistake is assuming every fever is the same. Fever is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and it can be caused by viruses, bacteria or other conditions. The appropriate treatment therefore depends on the cause. Before taking an antibiotic because someone says it worked for them during the previous monsoon, doctors advise patients to get the illness properly assessed and take antibiotics only when prescribed or recommended by a qualified medical professional. news.content: parliament monsoon sessionimdsupreme courtstrait of hormuz ❯ E हिं অ বাং ગુ ಕ മ म ଓ ਪੰ த తె ار ❯ National English हिंदी उत्तर प्रदेशउत्तराखंडछत्तीसगढ़झारखंडदिल्लीबिहारमध्य प्रदेशराजस्थानहरियाणाहिमाचल प्रदेश অসমীয়া বাংলা ગુજરાતી ಕನ್ನಡ മലയാളം मराठी ଓଡିଆ ਪੰਜਾਬੀ தமிழ் తెలుగు ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్తెలంగాణ اردو Live NATIONAL WORLD SPORTS ENTERTAINMENT OPINION PHOTOS HEALTH STATE BUSINESS More Live ETV Bharat / health Physicians Explain Why Antibiotics Aren’t the Answer To Every Monsoon Fever Monsoon fevers can be caused by several different infections. The problem is that antibiotics do not work against every one of them. Antibiotics are no cure-all in monsoon (Getty Images) By ETV Bharat Health Team Published : August 17, 2026 at 2:42 PM IST | Updated : August 17, 2026 at 2:47 PM IST 4 Min Read The rainy season has a familiar medical routine: someone develops a fever, someone else recommends an antibiotic, and within hours a strip of tablets appears on the kitchen counter. But doctors say this seemingly harmless habit can backfire. Monsoon fevers can be caused by several different infections, including dengue, chikungunya, malaria, typhoid, influenza and leptospirosis. The problem is that antibiotics do not work against every one of them. In fact, taking antibiotics when they are not needed can create another health problem: antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Fever Does Not Automatically Mean You Need An Antibiotic Dr Prerna Goyal, Sr Consultant - Physician, RG Hospitals in Ludhiana, says, “Monsoon brings a predictable rise in several types of fever. Yet many people automatically reach for antibiotics. The problem is that most monsoon fevers are viral. Dengue and chikungunya, for example, are mosquito-borne viral infections. Antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses. So taking an antibiotic for dengue or chikungunya does nothing to treat the virus causing the illness.” It is like trying to fix a Wi-Fi problem by changing the car's engine oil. The medicine may be real, but it is solving an entirely different problem. Dr Goyal says this habit of self-medicating is common during the monsoon. Patients sometimes arrive after taking antibiotics on their own for a week. By then, the doctor isn't simply treating the original illness. They also have to work around the effects of medication that may never have been necessary in the first place. Dengue and chikungunya are transmitted by mosquitoes and have no bacterial component that antibiotics can target. So if someone develops fever along with symptoms such as a rash or joint pain, the answer should not automatically be an antibiotic. Dr Goyal says such symptoms should prompt appropriate testing for conditions such as dengue or chikungunya. The first job is to find out what is causing the fever. Only then can the right treatment begin. An antibiotic does not help when a fever is caused by a virus (Getty Images) Even Bacterial Infections Need the Right Antibiotic Not every fever is viral. Some infections, including typhoid, are bacterial and may require antibiotics. But that does not mean taking any antibiotic from the medicine cabinet is a good idea. Dr Goyal points out that prescribing the wrong antibiotic — or starting the right antibiotic too early, before proper diagnosis — can mask symptoms, make accurate testing more difficult and contribute to antimicrobial resistance. In other words, even when an antibiotic is eventually required, guessing the antibiotic is not the same as treating the infection. Antibiotics Can Cause Problems When You Don't Need Them Dr Niraj Kumar, Senior Consultant, Internal Medicine, ShardaCare - HealthCity, says many people assume antibiotics will make a monsoon fever disappear faster. “But when the fever is caused by a virus, an antibiotic does not help. Unnecessary medicines can also cause side effects and contribute to antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This happens when bacteria gradually become resistant to medicines designed to kill them or stop their growth. The result is a future in which infections that were once relatively easy to treat can become much harder to manage. Also read: Drug-Resistant Infections Becoming A Major Global Health Threat: WHO Action Plan What Should You Do When Fever Starts? The first step is not necessarily to reach for an antibiotic. It is to observe the symptoms and assess the situation. Dr Kumar recommends rest, proper hydration and monitoring in cases of viral illness. Dr Goyal says fever that persists for more than two to three days should be medically evaluated, with blood tests considered before starting medication when appropriate. Fever accompanied by a rash or significant joint pain may require testing for dengue or chikungunya. Other symptoms and the patient's medical history can point doctors towards different causes. The important thing is that the treatment should follow the diagnosis, not the other way around. Any fever that lasts more than 48-72 hours deserves a visit to the doctor, especially if it’s not getting better or there are other worrying symptoms. Dr Kumar advises people to seek medical help quickly if fever persists or warning symptoms develop. Don't Treat Every Fever The Same Way The biggest mistake is assuming that every fever is the same. A fever is a symptom, not a diagnosis. It can be caused by a virus, bacteria or other conditions. The treatment depends on the cause. So before taking an antibiotic because someone in the family says, “This worked for me last monsoon,” pause. Get the illness assessed. Take antibiotics only when a doctor determines that they are needed. It does not report any confirmed outbreak or specific case numbers but serves as a public health advisory on responsible antibiotic use during the monsoon season.

news.content: Health & Fitness Virus-Transmitting, Invasive Mosquitoes Discovered In Contra Costa County The mosquitoes can transmit Zika, dengue fever, yellow fever, and chikungunya. Bay City News , News Partner Posted Sun, Aug 16, 2026 at 6:44 pm PT Read More BRENTWOOD, CA — A type of invasive mosquito that can potentially spread viruses from person to person was recently detected in another city in Contra Costa County. County officials confirmed Friday that mosquitoes had been trapped in the city of Brentwood that were of the type Aedes aegypti, which have also been detected in Antioch over the past three years, when they became known in California. County officials launched a program in July to release male Aedes aegypti treated with bacteria that will produce sterile eggs when they mate with females. Find out what's happening in Concord for free with the latest updates from Patch. Male mosquitoes do not bite, so there is no risk to humans, according to county health officials. Female Aedes aegypti are aggressive biters of humans and can pester hosts more than other types of mosquitoes, even in small numbers. Find out what's happening in Concord for free with the latest updates from Patch. They can also transmit potentially dangerous viruses such as Zika, dengue fever, yellow fever, and chikungunya. That has made eradicating them a priority for the Contra Costa Mosquito and Vector Control District, which leads pest control efforts in the county. Even small amounts of water can serve as breeding grounds for mosquitoes. Officials recommend regularly inspecting properties for standing water and dumping or draining any that is found. The mosquitoes in Brentwood were found because of a call from a resident. District officials urged anyone who encounters biting insects to report them online or (925) 685-9301. news.content: CubaHeadlines Guantánamo Acknowledges Rising Aedes Aegypti Numbers, Highlights Failures in Detecting Fever Cases Friday, August 14, 2026 by Edward Lopez The municipalities of Guantánamo, Caimanera, San Antonio del Sur, El Salvador, and Niceto Pérez have the highest concentration of mosquitoes - Image © Venceremos Officials from both the political and health sectors in Guantánamo acknowledged on Friday that the province is facing a worsening epidemiological situation, characterized by a surge in the presence of the Aedes aegypti mosquito and shortcomings in identifying fever cases. Health Yoel Pérez García, the first secretary of the Communist Party in the region, called a meeting with health directors, which also included Governor Alis Azahares Torreblanca. He demanded increased efforts in the anti-vector campaign, according to the official newspaper Venceremos. Pérez identified the shortage of field researchers as a critical issue. He emphasized that having a complete team is "crucial" for improving fever case detection and controlling the breeding sites of the mosquito, although the media refrained from providing specific statistics. The governor stressed "the importance of effective leadership and cross-sector collaboration to defeat such a dangerous vector, which is responsible for potentially deadly diseases like dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, and Zika." Most Impacted Areas Discover more Insects & Entomology Infectious Diseases Health Conditions Guantánamo, Caimanera, San Antonio del Sur, El Salvador, and Niceto Pérez have been identified as the most severely affected municipalities by the Aedes aegypti. Authorities in these areas are prioritizing health forums and educational talks to guide the public on eliminating breeding sites and seeking medical advice if fever symptoms arise. InfectiousDiseases Concerns Over Maternal and Child Health During the same meeting, there was a critical evaluation of the Maternal and Child Health Program's performance so far this year, with significant negative impacts noted in Guantánamo, Baracoa, Manuel Tames, and El Salvador. This alert follows weeks of ongoing decline. By late July, Guantánamo concluded a week with 23 suspected dengue cases, and the municipalities of Imías and San Antonio del Sur were placed on epidemiological alert, the highest risk level within the Cuban endemic channel before an epidemic is declared. On August 10, Radio Guantánamo reported an increase in fever cases in the provincial capital, with 18 suspected dengue cases mainly in the southern area, alongside confirmed circulation of serotypes 2, 3, and 4 of the virus. Nationwide Health Crisis Context Provincial challenges are part of a broader national health crisis. In June, Carilda Peña, deputy minister of Public Health, publicly warned that Cuba might face a new dengue epidemic due to the simultaneous circulation of all four virus serotypes. Structural factors are exacerbating the issue. Prolonged power outages force families to store water in containers that become mosquito breeding grounds. Additionally, the collapse of waste collection services due to fuel shortages aids mosquito proliferation, while a lack of insecticides hinders fumigation efforts across much of the country. Discover more Pest Control Content marketing services Political history books Guantánamo has a recurring history as one of the provinces hardest hit by dengue. In October 2022, it was identified as the first area in the country with infections, with nearly 1,600 Aedes aegypti larvae sites found in more than 1,300 homes across nine municipalities. InfectiousDiseases According to the Pan American Health Organization, Cuba ended 2025 with over 81,900 cases of dengue and chikungunya, and at least 65 deaths linked to these diseases—figures that the Ministry of Public Health took months to publicly acknowledge. Key Questions About the Aedes Aegypti Outbreak in Guantánamo What measures are being taken to combat the Aedes aegypti outbreak in Guantánamo? Authorities are prioritizing anti-vector campaigns, increasing the number of field researchers, and conducting health forums and educational talks to guide the public on eliminating mosquito breeding sites and recognizing fever symptoms. Why is Guantánamo particularly affected by dengue? Guantánamo's vulnerability is exacerbated by structural issues like prolonged power outages, ineffective waste management, and a shortage of insecticides, which create favorable conditions for mosquito proliferation. How does the national health crisis in Cuba relate to the situation in Guantánamo? The problems in Guantánamo are part of a larger national health crisis, with the simultaneous circulation of all dengue serotypes and significant structural challenges affecting the entire country. analysis.brief_en: Guantánamo officials announced on August 14, 2026 that the province is experiencing a surge in Aedes aegypti mosquito populations and persistent difficulties in detecting fever cases. Health secretary Yoel Pérez García convened a meeting with health directors and Governor Alis Azahares Torreblanca, urging intensified anti‐vector actions, increased recruitment of field researchers, and broader health education on eliminating breeding sites. The governor emphasized that the mosquito can transmit deadly diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika, though specific local case numbers are unavailable; only 23 suspected dengue cases and 18 suspected fever cases have been reported in the capital to date. Nationally, Cuba recorded over 81,900 combined dengue and chikungunya cases and at least 65 deaths in 2025, indicating a high risk of further transmission. Ongoing structural challenges—including frequent power outages, poor waste management, and limited insecticide supplies—complicate control efforts, and the lack of precise local statistics hampers assessment of the true burden.
